summary:
Indiana is a state of the United States, and a trans visitor here stands under the national framework on passports, visas, entry screening and federal custody, which the country record carries. What follows is the state layer.

Indiana's Bureau of Motor Vehicles ban on gender-marker changes to driver's licences and state identification cards took effect on 1 February 2026. It ended the route residents had used to obtain such a change, which ran through a court-ordered gender change or a physician's statement. The ban completed an administrative rule change the bureau initiated; LGBTQ advocates who testified against it said it would forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents whose documents no longer match how they present. The ACLU has challenged the policy in court.

Governor Mike Braun's March 2025 executive order defining sex solely as assigned sex at birth directed the Indiana Department of Health to stop updating gender markers, and the bureau's 2026 rule extended that prohibition to licences and identification cards. Birth-certificate changes had been available by court order from 2014 until 2025. In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined in split votes to hear two cases brought by transgender girls seeking amended birth certificates, which left appellate rulings standing that trial courts have no authority to grant a change unless the General Assembly codifies it. One of those cases involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation her school used to restrict her bathroom access.

Indiana issued an X marker between March 2019 and January 2020, on presentation of an amended birth certificate or a physician's statement confirming permanent gender change. The bureau withdrew it after a public hearing, and a March 2020 opinion from the attorney general held that only the General Assembly could authorise nonbinary designations.

As of April 2026, Indiana law places no restriction on transgender people using restrooms that match their gender identity, and Indianapolis and Bloomington ordinances expressly protect that use. Proposals to criminalise it have died in committee since 2021, and in August 2023 a Seventh Circuit decision upheld a preliminary injunction barring schools from limiting a transgender student's bathroom use while litigation continued.

Senate Bill 182 passed the Indiana Senate 37-8 on 27 January 2026 on a party-line vote and went to the House. It would define sex and gender by reproductive biology at birth, permanently bar amendments to birth certificates, require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females as assigned at birth, and confine prison housing to a placement matching birth sex. Its author, Senator Liz Brown of Fort Wayne, said the proposal protects women's private spaces; opponents including GenderNexus warned that a provision allowing anyone directly or indirectly injured to sue a school would encourage harassment-style enforcement. The bill received no House hearing and is not law.

Gender-affirming care for minors is barred. Senate Bill 480, passed and signed in 2023 under an emergency clause, prohibits physicians from providing gender-transition procedures to anyone under 18 or from aiding such care, with a phase-out for existing patients. It was enjoined on 16 June 2023, took effect on 27 February 2024 after a stay, and was upheld in November 2024. The ban covers surgery, puberty blockers and hormone therapy. A trans visitor under 18 cannot obtain that care in Indiana.

Indiana's hate-crimes law, enacted in April 2019, allows harsher sentences where an offence was motivated by a victim's perceived or actual characteristics, gender identity among them. It creates an aggravating circumstance rather than a standalone offence; the state had tracked bias crimes without any sentencing enhancement from 2003 until then.
tangentialFactors:
Erin In The Morning's February 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map places Indiana among the harshest anti-trans states in the country, citing the 2026 identification policy and the bathroom-ban legislation as the drivers of risk for adults.

Treatment inside Indiana varies by locality. The ordinances protecting restroom use in Indianapolis and Bloomington, and the employment protections in Marion, Monroe, Tippecanoe and Vanderburgh counties and numerous cities, have no statewide counterpart, and the state-level direction runs the other way.
localsOnly:
Indiana has recognised and performed marriages between people of the same sex since October 2014, when the federal district ruling in Baskin v. Bogan took effect after the U.S. Supreme Court declined the appeal on 6 October 2014. Annual attempts to amend the state constitution to bar such marriages ended then.

No Indiana statute lists gender identity or sexual orientation as a protected employment category. Protection for state employees rests on executive orders from 2004 and 2005. Ordinances in Marion, Monroe, Tippecanoe and Vanderburgh counties and in numerous cities prohibit employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression; Lake County, Fort Wayne and Whitestown cover sexual orientation only. In Hively v. Ivy Tech, decided 8-3 on 4 April 2017, the Seventh Circuit held that employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is sex discrimination under Title VII, binding in Indiana; that holding addresses sexual orientation rather than gender identity.

House Bill 1569, signed in April 2023 and effective 1 July 2023, bars the use of state or federal funds for sexual reassignment surgery for incarcerated patients, exempting approvals granted before that date.

House Bill 1608, signed in May 2023, bars classroom instruction on human sexuality in kindergarten through third grade and requires schools to notify a parent in writing when a non-emancipated minor asks to be called a different name, pronoun or title.

A May 2023 law bars city and county governments from enacting conversion-therapy bans by ordinance or executive order, so the practice remains legal across the state.

Indiana decriminalised sexual activity between people of the same sex effective 1 July 1977, and the age of consent is 16. The earlier statute carried penalties of two to 14 years and, at an earlier period, death; a House committee rejected 6-4 a 1977 proposal to reinstate consensual sodomy as a felony.

The Religious Freedom Restoration Act signed on 26 March 2015 drew boycott threats and protests over its effect on LGBT people, and a clarification on 2 April 2015 provided that it does not authorise providers to refuse services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the April 2015 clarification of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act covers gender identity or only sexual orientation is stated inconsistently across the sources consulted, so the question is unresolved here.

No enforcement data was found on how often gender-identity bias is charged as an aggravating circumstance under the 2019 hate-crimes law.

The ACLU challenge to the Bureau of Motor Vehicles gender-marker ban is pending and its outcome is not recorded.

The sources document restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors in Indiana but say nothing about the availability of such care to adults in the state.

Senate Bill 182 passed the Senate on 27 January 2026 and received no House hearing; its prospects in a later session are not sourced.
